drip.author: maplebound
drip.title: Fall colour season is starting and I'm prepared to defend Ontario maples against the entire country
drip.body:
Drove up the valley on the weekend and the red maples in the low wet spots are already going, the way they always do, a week or two ahead of everything else. By the Thanksgiving long weekend the whole valley will look like it's on fire in the nicest possible way.

I know every province thinks it does autumn best. I'm open to hearing your case. I'm just not going to agree with it.

comments.author: chinook_wind
comments.body: Larches. Up in the Rockies the larches go gold for a couple of weeks in late September and then drop every needle like they were never there. A conifer that changes colour and then leaves is a better plot than anything a maple has ever done. Only downside is half of Alberta has the same idea on the same weekend.

replies.author: maplebound
replies.body: A tree that goes gold and then ghosts you. I'll admit that's strong material. Still not agreeing.

comments.author: stormglass
comments.body: Cape Breton in October. The Cabot Trail with the highlands gone red and orange right down to the ocean, and fiddles going in every hall along the way, because the whole island throws a music festival for the occasion. You bring a maple, I bring a maple with a sea view and a soundtrack.

replies.author: bluenoser_belle
replies.body: Correct answer, and I say that as a mainland Nova Scotian who resents how much credit Cape Breton gets. Resents it lovingly. From Halifax.

comments.author: northof60
comments.body: Up here it's already done. The birches went yellow for about ten days, the bearberry on the rocks went red, and that was autumn. Blink and you miss it. But that red ground cover running off toward the horizon is something I wish more people got to see.

comments.author: regina_mona
comments.body: Prairie autumn isn't trees, it's the whole field. The stubble goes gold, the aspen bluffs go yellow, and the evening sun comes in so low it lights everything up sideways. You have to look wide instead of up.

replies.author: maplebound
replies.body: Look wide instead of up is a lovely way to put it. I'll call that one a draw, which from me is basically a concession.

drip.author: prairiedialup
drip.title: combine went past the house at 11pm with every light on. looked like a cruise ship lost at sea
drip.body: harvest is on. haven't seen the neighbours in daylight in a week. you just hear them. rumbling. at all hours

comments.author: regina_mona
comments.body: The lights out in the fields this time of year are my favourite constellation. From the highway you can see three or four combines working a section in the dark, all moving slow, like they're thinking something over.

comments.author: portage_and_main
comments.body: Manitoba harvest checking in. The grain trucks on the highway are the real test of character. You follow one for twenty minutes, he pulls onto the shoulder to let you by, you both wave. That's the whole country right there.

replies.author: prairiedialup
replies.body: the wave is mandatory. two fingers off the wheel minimum. anything less and word gets around

comments.author: tundrabloom
comments.body: There's something lovely about a whole region staying up late to bring a season in. Meanwhile my own harvest this week was one colander of beans and I felt like a farmer.

drip.author: codfather
drip.title: Out on the barrens for partridgeberries this morning, and no, I'm not telling you where
drip.body:
Bit early yet, they sweeten up after the first frost, but the patch was red enough that I couldn't stand to wait. Came home with a full ice cream bucket, wet knees, and a sunburn on the back of my neck in September, which is an achievement in itself out here.

Every family on the island has a berry spot passed down like an heirloom. Me father showed me ours and swore me to secrecy. Anyone who comes along with me now has to keep their eyes shut for the last stretch of road.

comments.author: bluenoser_belle
comments.body: Nova Scotia is the same with blueberries. My aunt will drive you to her spot and take three different back roads so you can't find it again. We've been going for years and I still couldn't point to it on a map.

replies.author: codfather
replies.body: Your aunt would do well out here, my dear. Three back roads is proper tradecraft.

comments.author: chinook_wind
comments.body: Calgary's version is saskatoon berries, and those are long done by now, but it's the same code. You don't post the spot, and you don't bring anybody who'd post the spot.

comments.author: ferndalefog
comments.body: West coast question: is a partridgeberry just a lingonberry with a Newfoundland accent? Because I've been buying lingonberry jam at the Swedish furniture store for years and I'm starting to suspect I've been had.

replies.author: codfather
replies.body: Same berry, different passport, b'y. Jam, muffins, and a bag in the freezer for February when you need reminding the sun exists. Your jar's fine. It's just never seen a barren.

drip.author: northof60
drip.title: First real aurora of the season and I watched the whole thing from the kitchen in my socks
drip.body:
It's dark enough at night again, finally. Went to put the kettle on a little while ago and the sky over the rooftops was moving. Green, a little pink along the bottom edge, the whole slow curtain routine.

I've lived here long enough that I should be used to it. Stood at the window long enough that the tea went cold. Not used to it.

comments.author: regina_mona
comments.body: We get them down here too, a few times a season, and every time somebody in town posts 'is anyone else seeing this' like we're all passing around a rumour. Saskatchewan at least has the flat horizon for it.

comments.author: stormglass
comments.body: All my years in the Maritimes and I've seen them exactly twice, both times so faint I had to take somebody else's word for it. Socks at the kitchen window sounds like the right way to do it.

replies.author: northof60
replies.body: Come up in February. I'll lend you socks, and you won't need anybody's word for it.

comments.author: prairiedialup
comments.body: the tea going cold is how you know it was a good one

drip.author: tundrabloom
drip.title: The equinox lands this evening, and I'm choosing to call it a tie
drip.body:
Twelve hours of light and twelve of dark, give or take some fine print. From here the dark gets a little more of the day, every day, until December, and I won't pretend I love that part.

But the garlic goes in soon, and planting something in the fall that you won't see until spring is the most stubborn kind of hope I know. So: a tie. I'll take a tie.

comments.author: northof60
comments.body: Up here we're losing about six minutes of daylight a day right now. You can feel it go. By the time you notice supper is in the dark, it's been in the dark for a week.

comments.author: GalaxyBrainGwen
comments.body: The fine print is my favourite part! The day with genuinely equal light and dark comes a few days after the equinox, because the atmosphere bends sunlight over the horizon and sunrise is counted from the top edge of the sun, not the middle. So on the equinox itself you get a few bonus minutes. The tie goes to the light.

replies.author: tundrabloom
replies.body: The tie goes to the light. That's getting stitched onto something.

comments.author: stormglass
comments.body: My grandmother called this week 'the turn' and started the first pot of soup of the season on principle, whatever the weather was doing. I've kept that one. There's a pot on as I type.

comments.author: crokinole_king
comments.body: At my place the equinox also marks the official start of game night season. The dark gets more of the day, the crokinole board gets more of the evening. I call that a fair trade.

drip.author: chinook_wind
drip.title: Calgary's forecast this week goes 24, 22, snow, 19, and nobody at work even looked up
drip.body:
Wore shorts to walk the dog on Tuesday. Friday says wet snow. By Sunday it's back up near twenty. I've already moved the patio chairs in and back out once.

The trees are halfway to yellow, the tomatoes are still hanging on, and there's a very real chance they'll all be wearing snow by tomorrow night. September out here is less a season than a coin toss.

comments.author: portage_and_main
comments.body: Winnipeg respects the chaos but can't match it. When our weather turns, it at least picks a direction and sticks with it until April, out of pure stubbornness.

comments.author: ferndalefog
comments.body: Vancouver forecast this week: rain, rain, showers, rain. No drama, just commitment. I'd trade you one snow day for a single dry Saturday.

replies.author: chinook_wind
replies.body: Deal, but my snow melts by Sunday and your rain is signed through March.

comments.author: penaltyboxphil
comments.body: Snow in September is just the outdoor rink sending a text. Not coming yet. Just letting you know it's thinking about you.

comments.author: codfather
comments.body: Calgary gets one snow day and it's over by Sunday? My son, in St. John's we get snow in May and fog in June, and then one hot afternoon in August that we talk about until Christmas. You're doing grand.

comments.author: tundrabloom
comments.body: Get a sheet over those tomatoes tonight. And if you lose the fight, pick them all green and put them in a paper bag with a banana. Half of them will ripen on the counter out of pure spite.

replies.author: chinook_wind
replies.body: Update: it snowed. The sheet held, the banana is on the job, and the patio chairs are back inside for the second time this week.

drip.author: stormglass
drip.title: Annapolis Valley apple run: one peck, two pies, and a pumpkin nobody in this house asked for
drip.body:
Drove out to the Valley this morning with the dog in the back seat. The Honeycrisp are on, the McIntosh are on, and the whole orchard had that cold, sweet smell that I'm convinced is what September would be if it were a person.

Picked far more than this household will ever eat and made two pies before the enthusiasm wore off. The pumpkin just happened. I don't remember choosing it. It rode home in the front seat like it had always lived here.

comments.author: bluenoser_belle
comments.body: My husband and I made the same drive last fall and came home with enough apples to open a small shop. Every September he announces 'this year we're only getting one bag.' He has never once got one bag.

comments.author: maplebound
comments.body: Valley versus Valley, then. The orchards out our way are doing the same thing this weekend and I also came home with more apples than sense. No pumpkin, though. I'm told they only choose you when you're ready.

replies.author: stormglass
replies.body: It chose me. I've made my peace with it. It has a spot by the door now.

comments.author: tundrabloom
comments.body: Zone 3 apples are small, tart, and have survived winters your Honeycrisp can only have nightmares about. I love them the way you love a scrappy dog. The pie is still very good.

comments.author: salt_beef_bucket
comments.body: Newfoundland doesn't do orchards the way you crowd on the mainland do, so every fall I'm just jealous of the rest of the Atlantic. I'd trade a jar of partridgeberry jam for a slice of that pie, sight unseen.

drip.author: portage_and_main
drip.title: Thanksgiving is two weeks out. What's the one dish your family would riot without?
drip.body:
The group chat started this morning. Nobody has asked who's hosting yet, but three separate people have already confirmed they're bringing the same squash thing. That's how you know it's the real menu.

Ours is cabbage rolls sitting right beside the turkey like they've got every right to be there, because they do. What's yours?

comments.author: salt_beef_bucket
comments.body: Jiggs dinner, with the turkey riding along as a guest. Salt beef in the pot, pease pudding in the bag, turnip, cabbage, and the gravy that ties it all together. The turkey is welcome. The turkey is not in charge.

replies.author: portage_and_main
replies.body: 'The turkey is not in charge' might be the most Canadian sentence ever written about a holiday.

comments.author: crokinole_king
comments.body: Pie isn't up for debate, it's pumpkin and there's no vote. What actually gets negotiated at our place is the Mario Kart bracket after dinner. My brother-in-law has already started the trash talk in the chat. Two weeks early. He's nervous.

comments.author: bluenoser_belle
comments.body: My mother makes a pot of seafood chowder to 'tide everyone over' while the bird finishes, and then acts shocked when nobody has room for turkey. Every year. Same shock.

comments.author: prairiedialup
comments.body: saskatchewan answer is a jellied salad nobody under 60 eats and nobody over 60 will let us retire

replies.author: regina_mona
replies.body: Can confirm the salad. My grandmother's has tiny marshmallows suspended in it like a museum exhibit, and we are not permitted to ask questions.

late_comments.author: prairiedialup
late_comments.body: found this looking for somewhere to go before it snows. the cypress hills. part saskatchewan, part alberta, and the highest ground between the rockies and labrador. there are hills out here. nobody believes me. more room for me

late_comments.author: ferndalefog
late_comments.body: Reading this at 7:30 on a September evening with the lamps already on, and it reads like science fiction. Mowing the lawn at midnight in daylight. Imagine.

late_comments.author: penaltyboxphil
late_comments.body: Found this after the exact same argument broke out in a rink lobby at 6 a.m. on Saturday. Old fashioned plain, dunked in arena coffee. It's the only one in the box built to survive the dunk.
